L312:          The Company has  identified  several key  industries or facility  types
L313: that it believes  have  substantial  and  increasing  requirements  for security
L314: services,  including  telecommunication  and  technology  companies,   corporate
L315: complexes and industries and facilities for which security  systems are required
L316: by regulation.  The Company has developed expertise in the security  regulations
L317: applicable to airports, pharmaceutical companies, prisons and nuclear utilities.
L318:          The  Company's  marketing  strategy  emphasizes   developing  long-term
L319: relationships with clients so that the Company can provide  additional  services
L320: as the clients' security requirements evolve. The Company undertakes significant
L321: pre-assessment  of a  prospective  client's  needs before an initial  contact is
L322: made. A long-term  relationship  typically  begins with an engagement to provide
L323: consulting  and  planning  or  maintenance  and  technical   support   services.
L324: Consulting  and  planning  assignments  place  the  Company  in an  advantageous
L325: position,  often as the client's project manager, to be engaged to implement the
L326: plan ultimately adopted by the client. Engagements for maintenance and technical
L327: support  enable the Company to identify  new  requirements  as they arise and to
L328: offer its solutions to such requirements.
L329:          The Company  employs a variety of pricing  strategies for its services.
L330: Proposals  for  consulting  services  are priced  based on an  estimate of hours
L331: multiplied by standard rates.  Systems integration  engagements are priced based
L332: upon  the  estimated  cost  of  the  components  of  the  engagement,  including
L333: subcontractors and equipment,  plus a profit margin. Pricing for engineering and
L334: maintenance  services vary widely depending on the scope of the specific project
L335: and the length of engagement. All proposals are reviewed by the Company's senior
L336: management.
L337:          Many projects require that the primary  contractor obtain a performance
L338: bond in the amount of the  contract.  The amount of bonding  that the Company is
L339: able to obtain depends upon the level of its working capital and net worth.  The
L340: Company  believes that prior to the initial public  offering of its common stock
L341: in October  1997,  its  ability to compete  for larger  projects as a primary or
L342: independent  contractor,  rather  than  through a joint  venture or  subcontract
L343: arrangement,  was constrained by its inability to obtain adequate  bonding.  The
L344: Company has since secured bonding with a major surety that will enable it to bid
L345: as a primary contractor on larger contracts.
L346:          The  Company  is  evaluating  several   opportunities  to  expand  into
L347: international  operations,  which it  anticipates  it will  initially  undertake
L348: through joint ventures or partnerships with local and international companies.
L349:

L386:          During 1999,  MCI WorldCom,  Inc.  ("MCI"),  Kodak and the U.S.  Postal
L387: Service  accounted  for  33%,  9%  and  7% of  the  Company's  earned  revenues,
L388: respectively. The loss of a significant portion of the revenue from any of these
L389: clients  would need to be replaced to avoid a material  adverse  effect upon the
L390: Company's  business,  operating  results and financial  condition.  Although MCI
L391: WorldCom  accounted for a substantial  portion of the  Company's  revenue,  work
L392: performed  for them was  comprised  of multiple  projects at numerous  different
L393: facilities.  Firm  contracts are already in place for a  significant  portion of
L394: revenue from MCI WorldCom in 2000. The Company has  diversified  its client base
L395: by winning several new clients regionally and nationally.  The revenues from new
L396: clients are  expected to more than  replace any  reduction  in revenue  from the
L397: existing clients.
L398: Competition
L399:          The security industry is highly competitive.  The Company competes on a
L400: local,  regional and national basis with systems  integrators,  consulting firms
L401: and  engineering  and design  firms.  The Company  believes  that it is the only
L402: provider offering its comprehensive  range of services on a national basis. As a
L403: result, the Company competes with different  companies depending upon the nature
L404: of the project and the services  being  offered.  For  example,  the Company has
L405: competed with Johnson Controls,  Science Applications  International Corporation
L406: and Sensormatic for systems  integration  work, and Lockwood Greene and Holmes &
L407: Narver for consulting and planning and  engineering and design work. Many of its
L408: competitors  have greater name  recognition  and  financial  resources  than the
L409: Company.  The Company's  competitors also include  equipment  manufacturers  and
L410: vendors  that also  provide  security  services.  The  Company  may face  future
L411: competition from potential new entrants into the security industry and increased
L412: competition from existing competitors that may attempt to develop the ability to
L413: offer the full range of services  offered by the Company.  The Company  believes
L414: that  competition  is based  primarily on the ability to deliver  solutions that
L415: effectively meet a client's  requirements  and, to a lesser extent and primarily
L416: in  competitive  bid  situations,  on price.  There can be no assurance that the
L417: Company will be able to compete  successfully in the future against  existing or
L418: potential competitors.

L424: Backlog
L425:          The  Company's  backlog  consists of confirmed  orders,  including  the
L426: balance of projects in process. The backlog also includes projects for which the
L427: Company  has been  notified  it is the  successful  bidder even though a binding
L428: agreement has not been executed.  Projects for which a binding  contract has not
L429: been executed may be canceled at any time. Binding contracts may also be subject
L430: to cancellation or postponement,  although cancellation  generally obligates the
L431: client to pay the costs incurred by the Company. Long-term maintenance contracts
L432: may be canceled  without cause.  As of December 31, 1998 and 1999, the Company's
L433: backlog was approximately $4.0 million and $4.2 million,  respectively.  Backlog
L434: as of December 31, 1999,  includes projects having a value of approximately $2.4
L435: million for which  binding  contracts  have not been executed and all backlog is
L436: expected to be completed  during 2000.  Backlog orders as of any particular date
L437: may not be indicative of actual operating  results for any fiscal period.  There
L438: can be no assurance that any amount of backlog will be realized.  In addition to
L439: backlog the Company has potential follow-on projects with its existing customers
L440: of another $14.8 million. These are projects which the Company has been informed
L441: that are likely to happen over the next 12 to 24 months.

L444: based in the Company's  headquarters located in Sterling,  Virginia. The balance
L445: work out of the company's regional offices. Eight of the Company's employees are

L486: Item 3.  Legal Proceedings.
L487:          Although the Company is a defendant in certain  suits  arising from the
L488: normal conduct of its business,  management does not believe that the resolution
L489: of  this  litigation  will  have a  material  adverse  effect  on the  Company's
L490: financial  position,  results of  operations,  or cash  flows.  This  litigation
L491: includes SecuraComm Consulting, Inc. v. Securacom, Incorporated. In this action,
L492: filed in the U.S. District Court for the district of New Jersey in October 1995,
L493: the plaintiff,  a consulting  company,  sought injunctive relief and damages for
L494: alleged  confusion  in the  marketplace  and lost  business  resulting  from the
L495: Company's alleged  infringement of plaintiff's claimed service mark. In November
L496: 1997,  the court ruled in favor of the  plaintiff  and enjoined the Company from
L497: using the name "Securacom,  Incorporated"  and awarded the plaintiff  damages in
L498: the amount of $1,900,000.  The Company appealed the decision and it was reversed
L499: in January 1999.  Attorneys'  fees in the amount of $262,000 were awarded to the
L500: plaintiff and the Company has appealed the award.

L358:          The Company has a very senior sales force, which has identified a
L359: significant number of near-term sales opportunities. With the cost reductions
L360: and initiatives described above in place, the Company is positioned to be more
L361: profitable, require less working capital and have much lower break-even point.
L362: If sufficient working capital is obtained to address outstanding debt with

L364: cash flow to execute enough additional business to achieve profitability going

L366:          The Company derives its revenues primarily from long-term, fixed-price
L367: contracts. Earnings are recognized based upon the Company's estimates of the
L368: cost and percentage of completion of individual contracts. Earned revenues equal
L369: the project's total contract amount multiplied by the proportion that direct
L370: project costs incurred on a project bear to estimated total direct project
L371: costs. Project costs include direct labor and benefits, direct material,
L372: subcontract costs, project related travel and other direct expenses.
L373:          Clients are invoiced based upon negotiated payment terms for each
L374: individual contract. Terms usually include a 25% down payment and the balance as
L375: stages of the work are completed. Maintenance contracts are billed either in
L376: advance, monthly, or quarterly. As a result, the Company records as an asset,
L377: costs and estimated earnings in excess of billings, and as a liability, billings
L378: in excess of costs and estimated earnings.

L472: Liquidity and Capital Resources
L473:          Through 1997, the Company funded its capital requirements with cash
L474: generated by operations, private equity offerings, and its initial public
L475: offering in October 1997. During April 1998, the Board of Directors approved the
L476: issuance of up to $2.0 million of convertible subordinated debentures to provide
L477: additional working capital. As of May 13, 1998, the Company had issued and sold
L478: $1,450,000 of debentures. The Company sold an additional $400,000 of debentures
L479: as of August 25, 1998. The debentures have an interest rate of 10%, are due on
L480: December 31, 1999 and are convertible into common stock of the Company at $8.50
L481: per share. In addition, the holders were issued 100 warrants for each $1,000 of
L482: investment with an exercise price of $2.50 and a term of three years.
L483:          During February 1999, the $1.9 million the Company was required to post

L485: trial court's judgment was reversed. The Company paid off $0.9 million of the
